summary: Having unified Japan, Toyotomi Hideyoshi planned to conquer Ming China and demanded passage through Korea. When the Joseon court refused, about 158,000 Japanese troops landed at Busan in May 1592. Armed with arquebuses and hardened by Japan's civil wars, they took Hanseong (Seoul) in less than three weeks and Pyongyang in July, while Katō Kiyomasa pushed into the far north-east. But Admiral Yi Sun-sin's navy won a string of victories that cut Japanese supply lines by sea, Korean Righteous Armies rose behind the lines, and in early 1593 a Ming army retook Pyongyang. The Japanese fell back to forts on the south coast while Ming and Japanese envoys negotiated. The talks collapsed in 1596, and in 1597 Hideyoshi sent a second invasion, which destroyed the Korean fleet but was halted short of Hanseong at Jiksan and at sea at Myeongnyang. Hideyoshi's death in September 1598 led Japan to withdraw; at Noryang in December Yi Sun-sin was killed in the last battle. The war devastated Korea and strained the Ming treasury.
casualties: Estimated at well over a million Korean civilian and military deaths, with tens of thousands of Koreans carried off to Japan, more than 100,000 Japanese and over 30,000 Ming soldiers killed, though all figures are uncertain.

brief.hook: Toyotomi Hideyoshi had just united Japan and dreamed of conquering China; when Korea refused to let his armies pass, he invaded it instead.

sides.who: The armies of Japan's lords, sent by Hideyoshi in nine divisions with labourers and sailors
The Joseon kingdom of Korea, its navy, and volunteer Righteous Armies of scholars, peasants and Buddhist monks
Ming China, Korea's overlord and protector, which sent armies and later a fleet

brief.resultLine: After Hideyoshi died in September 1598, Japan pulled its armies out; on 16 December Yi Sun-sin was killed at Noryang, the war's last battle.

strategies.name: Arquebus blitz
strategies.text: Veterans of Japan's civil wars, armed with many arquebuses, stormed Busan and raced north in three columns. They took the capital Hanseong in under three weeks and Pyongyang soon after.

strategies.name: Cutting the sea lanes
strategies.text: Admiral Yi Sun-sin's cannon-armed warships, led by turtle ships, wrecked Japanese fleets at Okpo and Hansan Island. Japan could no longer ship supplies up the west coast to its armies in the north.

strategies.name: The Ming relief army
strategies.text: In early 1593 a Ming army under Li Rusong joined Korean troops and monks to storm Pyongyang. Short of food, the Japanese abandoned the north and fell back to forts on the south coast.

impact: Korea was devastated: perhaps a million people died, farmland shrank sharply and tens of thousands were carried off to Japan.
The cost of the war strained the Ming treasury and helped weaken the dynasty, which fell in 1644.
The war weakened Hideyoshi's family, and Tokugawa Ieyasu took power in Japan as shogun in 1603.

sources.title: University of Texas at Austin, HIST 341K: Invasion of Korea

details: Having unified Japan, Toyotomi Hideyoshi demanded passage through Korea to conquer Ming China, and when the Joseon court refused he sent an army of about 158,800 soldiers, labourers and sailors in nine divisions. Konishi Yukinaga's First Division landed at Busan on 23 May 1592. The next day it stormed the fortress of Busanjin, commanded by Chŏng Pal, killing most of the garrison and many townspeople. Korea, at peace for two centuries, was badly prepared, and its defences in the south collapsed.

Konishi's troops moved on to the walled town of Dongnae just north of Busan. Its prefect, Song Sanghyŏn, refused to let them pass, and the town was stormed after hours of fighting; about 3,000 defenders were killed by Korean count. The other Japanese divisions landed behind the first, and three columns, under Konishi, Katō Kiyomasa and Kuroda Nagamasa, began a race north along separate roads towards the capital, Hanseong (Seoul).

The court sent General Yi Il south to stop the invaders on the central road, but he found only a few hundred raw troops at Sangju. On 3 June 1592 Konishi's veterans, armed with thousands of arquebuses, surrounded and destroyed his small army; Yi Il escaped and fled north. The Japanese musketeers, trained in the long civil wars of the Sengoku period, were far superior to Korean troops in open battle in the early months of the war.

General Sin Rip, Korea's most famous commander, chose not to hold the Choryong pass and instead deployed his cavalry on open ground at Tangeumdae, near Chungju, with rivers behind it. On 7 June 1592 Konishi's arquebusiers broke the Korean charges and drove the army into the rivers, where many drowned; Sin Rip took his own life. Chungju was the last organised defence before the capital, and King Seonjo fled north.

The court had already left Hanseong, and parts of the city, including the offices holding the slave registers, had been looted and burned by its own people. Konishi's division reached the capital first, on 10 June 1592, less than three weeks after landing, with Katō's division arriving soon after. King Seonjo withdrew to Pyongyang and later to Uiju on the Chinese border, and the Korean court appealed to the Ming emperor, its overlord, for help.

While Japan's armies swept north, the navy of Jeolla province under Admiral Yi Sun-sin sailed east from its base at Yeosu. On 16 June 1592 it surprised a Japanese transport fleet anchored at Okpo on Geoje island and destroyed 26 ships without losing one of its own. It was the first of a series of naval victories, won with sturdy panokseon warships and heavy cannon, that began to threaten the Japanese supply line from Busan.

A Korean army of about 10,000 held the north bank of the Imjin river, the barrier on the road from Hanseong to Pyongyang, and the Japanese waited there for two weeks without boats. Then the Japanese feigned a retreat; the Korean troops crossed in pursuit and were ambushed and destroyed on 6–7 July 1592. The road north lay open: Kato turned north-east into Hamgyong province, while Konishi and Kuroda marched on Pyongyang.

King Seonjo fled Pyongyang on 19 July 1592, and the panic his departure caused spread to the defenders. A Korean night attack across the Taedong river failed, and when the retreating troops showed the Japanese a ford, the defenders abandoned the city. Konishi's First Division entered Pyongyang on 24 July and found its granaries intact. Konishi halted there, waiting for supplies and reinforcements that the Korean navy and guerrilla attacks were making ever harder to deliver.

Hideyoshi ordered his admirals to destroy the Korean navy. Wakisaka Yasuharu's fleet of about 73 ships was lured out of the narrow strait of Gyeonnaeryang into open water off Hansan Island, where Yi Sun-sin's 56 warships, including turtle ships, closed round it in a crane-wing formation. On 15 August 1592 most of the Japanese fleet was destroyed. Hansan ended Japanese plans to supply their armies by sea along the west coast.

The Ming court was busy with a revolt at Ningxia, but it sent a small force of about 6,000 men under General Zu Chengxun across the Yalu. On 23 August 1592 it attacked Pyongyang in heavy rain, broke into the city and was cut to pieces in the streets by Konishi's musketeers; Zu escaped with a few survivors. The defeat convinced the Ming that a much larger army would be needed, while envoys bought time with truce talks.

Katō Kiyomasa's Second Division of more than 20,000 men crossed to the east coast, took Hamhung, the capital of Hamgyong province, and beat the provincial army at Songjin on 23 August. On 30 August it entered Hoeryong near the Tumen river, where two Korean princes and the governor had already been seized by local people and handed over. Katō even raided across the Tumen against the Jurchens. But Korean partisans soon rose across Hamgyong and retook its northern towns.

Jinju guarded the road from Gyeongsang into the rich province of Jeolla, which had escaped invasion and fed the Korean war effort. About 30,000 Japanese troops besieged the fortress, held by Kim Si-min with some 3,800 soldiers and a few thousand irregulars and 170 newly made arquebuses. After six days of assaults with siege towers and ladders the Japanese gave up on 13 November, having lost heavily; Kim Si-min was mortally wounded. Jinju became a symbol of Korean resistance, alongside the Righteous Armies.

In January 1593 a Ming army of about 40,000 under Li Rusong crossed the Yalu and, with Korean troops and monk soldiers, reached Pyongyang on 5 February. Its cannon battered the walls, and after three days of assaults Konishi abandoned the city on the night of 8 February and retreated south, losing thousands of men. The Japanese gave up most of the north. Katō Kiyomasa, in danger of being cut off, withdrew from Hamgyong province in the following weeks.

Confident after Pyongyang, Li Rusong pushed on towards Hanseong with an advance force, mostly cavalry. At the post station of Byeokjegwan, north of the capital, on 27 February 1593 it ran into a much larger Japanese army under Kobayakawa Takakage and was driven back with heavy losses in the mud. Li withdrew to Kaesong and then Pyongyang, and the two sides settled into a stalemate along the line from Kaesong to Hanseong.

General Kwon Yul fortified the hill fort of Haengjusanseong on the Han river west of Hanseong with about 2,300 soldiers, monks and townspeople. On 14 March 1593 some 30,000 Japanese attacked it in waves through the day, but the defenders, using cannon, rocket carts and stones, held out until the Japanese withdrew. Haengju, with Korean naval raids and the Ming burning of Japanese grain stores at Yongsan, left the army in Hanseong short of food.

Short of food, hit by disease and harassed by guerrillas, the Japanese commanders agreed in peace talks with the Ming envoy Shen Weijing to evacuate the capital and withdraw to the Busan area, while the Ming army would also pull back. They left Hanseong in the spring of 1593 and retreated to a chain of castles, the wajō, built along the southern coast of Gyeongsang province from Ulsan to Geoje, which they held for the rest of the war.

Hideyoshi was determined to avenge the failure at Jinju. In July 1593 a Japanese army of about 90,000, the largest single force of the war, besieged the fortress, defended by a few thousand soldiers and crowded with civilians. After a week of assaults the walls were breached and the city fell on 27 July; the Japanese killed its defenders and much of its population, Korean sources counting 60,000 dead. They then withdrew to their coastal forts.

For three years Ming and Japanese negotiators, chiefly Shen Weijing and Konishi Yukinaga, misrepresented each side's demands to their masters in order to keep the truce. Hideyoshi expected Ming surrender of territory and a princess, while the Ming believed he had asked to become a tributary king. When the deception came out at his audience with the Ming envoys at Osaka Castle in 1596, Hideyoshi was enraged and ordered a second invasion of Korea.

In 1597 more than 140,000 Japanese troops crossed to Korea. Yi Sun-sin had been removed from his command after a Japanese plot, and his successor Won Gyun was ordered to attack the Japanese fleet. On 28 August 1597, off Geoje island near Chilcheollyang, his tired fleet was surprised at night by a much larger Japanese navy. Most of the Korean fleet, by one count 188 ships, was destroyed, and Won Gyun was killed. The sea route to the west coast now lay open to Japan.

Japan's second offensive aimed at Jeolla province, which had escaped the first invasion. The Left Army of about 50,000 under Ukita Hideie besieged Namwon, held by about 3,000 Ming soldiers under Yang Yuan and a few hundred Koreans. The town fell on the night of 26 September after four days; Yang Yuan broke out with about 100 men, but most of the defenders and many townspeople were killed. The Japanese went on to take Jeonju.

While the Left Army swept Jeolla, the Japanese Right Army under Mōri Hidemoto and Katō Kiyomasa marched north through Chungcheong towards Hanseong. On 16 October 1597 its vanguard under Kuroda Nagamasa met a Ming force of about 8,000 infantry and cavalry near Jiksan, south of the capital, and was driven back after a hard fight. Jiksan was the farthest the Japanese got towards Hanseong in the second invasion; with winter coming, their armies turned back towards the south coast.

Restored to command after Chilcheollyang, Yi Sun-sin had only 13 warships left. He waited for the Japanese fleet, at least 133 warships, in the narrow Myeongnyang strait off Jindo island, where a powerful tidal current runs. On 26 October 1597 his ships held the strait for hours, sinking or disabling about 30 Japanese vessels, and when the tide turned the Japanese withdrew. The victory stopped the Japanese navy from advancing along the west coast to support their armies.

The Japanese held the winter in new coastal castles, and the Ming general Yang Hao led about 50,000 Ming and Korean troops against the new Japanese castle at Ulsan. Its garrison held out through repeated assaults until a Japanese relief army arrived; on 19 February 1598 the allies broke off the siege and retreated with heavy losses. A stalemate followed along the south coast, from Ulsan to Suncheon.

Hideyoshi died at Fushimi Castle on 18 September 1598, leaving his five-year-old son Hideyori as heir. The Council of Five Elders that now governed Japan kept his death secret and ordered the armies in Korea home. Meanwhile allied armies attacked the Japanese castles at Sacheon and Suncheon in October 1598 and were beaten off, but the Japanese prepared to evacuate their forts and sail back to Japan.

Konishi Yukinaga was blockaded at Suncheon by the Korean and Ming fleets, and Shimazu Yoshihiro sailed with about 500 ships to rescue him. Yi Sun-sin and the Ming admiral Chen Lin intercepted the relief fleet in the Noryang strait before dawn on 16 December 1598 and destroyed about half of it. Yi was killed by a gunshot at the height of the battle. Konishi escaped round the south of Namhae island, and on 21 December the last Japanese commanders sailed from Busan for Japan.
